brief.head: Sugar-coated heroes
brief.text: We ad­mire Newton or Solzhenitsyn through their high­lights, Ajay Shah said. A mi­cro­scope on any free thinker’s life would ex­pose reck­less, im­pru­dent be­hav­iour. {061-C16}

brief.head: Gandhi, up close
brief.text: Gandhi’s *The Story of My Experiments with Truth*, Ajay Shah said, shows in great de­tail how he was “quite a weirdo”. {061-R22}

brief.head: The abolitionist test
brief.text: In Paul Graham’s essay, Princeton stu­dents all said they would have been abo­li­tion­ists in the deep South. That sim­ply isn’t true, Amit Varma said. {061-C17}

brief.head: Glisters, not glitters
brief.text: Clichés start with pi­o­neers: Fritz Lang’s *Metropolis* gave cin­ema many, Amit Varma said. Ajay Shah cor­rected a Shakespeare line: “All that glis­ters is not gold.” {061-J17}

brief.head: Moonshots, wanted

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the price of being early
lead.head: Right too early, damned for it

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 61

body: It is a cold win­ter af­ter­noon in early nine­teenth-century London. A girl sits by her mother’s grave be­hind St Pancras Church and traces the let­ters on the stone with a fin­ger. That, Amit Varma said, is how she learned to write. {061-S01}

Varma, who had writ­ten the scene him­self, read it out as a quiz for Ajay Shah. Shah guessed Mary Wollstonecraft. She was the mother. The girl was Mary Shelley, and both women, Varma said, wrote books that changed the world.
The mother had died of an in­fec­tion a few days after giv­ing birth. The daugh­ter would for­ever feel guilt that her birth had killed her mother.
Progress hap­pens re­ally slowly, Varma said. In every age some peo­ple think things that later seem com­pletely nor­mal but are rad­i­cal at the time.
“And often they are shunned and de­spised and treated in hor­ri­ble ways,” he said. The hosts called them the out­laws.
## A relay race of dates

Varma’s first three out­laws, he said, could be one in­ter­lock­ing web se­ries. Wollstonecraft read John Locke on equal rights for all men and asked where women stood. Horace Walpole called her a “hyena in pet­ti­coats”.
Mary Shelley wrote *Frankenstein* at eigh­teen, be­fore sci­ence fic­tion ex­isted as a genre. The typ­i­cal re­ac­tion was that her hus­band must have writ­ten it.

Ignaz Semmelweis, born in 1818, the year of *Frankenstein*, cut deaths in a Vienna ma­ter­nity ward by mak­ing doc­tors wash their hands. He could not ex­plain why it worked, and he died in a lu­natic asy­lum.

The threads tie to­gether. Wollstonecraft’s fatal in­fec­tion, Varma said, came from a doc­tor who had not washed his hands. Told in par­al­lel, “it be­gins and ends with hand wash­ing, it be­gins and ends with child­birth, it be­gins and ends in death”.
## Where is the mech­a­nism?
Shah an­swered with out­laws of sci­ence: Alfred Wegener, who saw that the con­ti­nents had drifted apart; Boltzmann, whose physics rested on atoms no­body had seen; the monk Mendel; and Darwin.

Their com­mon trou­ble, Shah said, was a miss­ing ex­pla­na­tion. Each had ev­i­dence and good pre­dic­tions but no ac­count of how. “Last mile prob­lem. Darwin did not have the ex­pla­na­tion. So this is a re­cur­rent theme we’ll see again and again.” {061-C07}
Varma reached for the Planck prin­ci­ple, that sci­ence changes one fu­neral at a time, and warned of sur­vivor bias: we re­mem­ber only the out­laws who were even­tu­ally vin­di­cated.
## Why so hos­tile?

What puz­zled Varma was the hos­til­ity. Drawing on an essay by Paul Graham, he said being con­ven­tional-minded is un­der­stand­able, but the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded are the great­est dan­ger. {061-C10}

Shah’s an­swer was the es­tab­lish­ment of in­sti­tu­tions, cre­den­tials, jour­nals, jobs and fund­ing. A dis­rup­tive idea threat­ens people’s own lives. “It’s the same as any other bu­reau­cracy,” he said. “What bu­reau­cra­cies want is to keep the boat going.” {061-C12}
He also of­fered a self­ish rem­edy. Since most peo­ple ig­nore mav­er­icks, lis­ten­ing to them is an ar­bi­trage op­por­tu­nity. “This is a $500 bill lying on the ground,” he said. {061-C13}
Better, he said, to spend an hour with a mad per­son than with a sane one. “That’s why I do the show with you,” Varma replied.
Shah ended with a place rather than a book: Boltzmann’s tomb­stone in Vienna, which bears the equa­tion S = k ln W.

second.label: The vaccine pioneer
second.head: Grant, grant, no, no, no
second.deck: Amit Varma on Katalin Karikó, rejected for years before mRNA vaccines
body: Katalin Karikó’s early re­search on mRNA was treated as a joke, Amit Varma said, some­thing on the fringes. She ap­plied for grant after grant, and every time the an­swer was no. {061-S13}

She ap­plied for a fac­ulty po­si­tion at the University of Pennsylvania and was told she was not of fac­ulty qual­ity. It took years, Varma said, until “the mo­ment met the woman”. mRNA vac­cines proved a mir­a­cle, and in a sense, he said, she saved the planet.

Varma then turned the story around. We re­mem­ber such peo­ple be­cause they were even­tu­ally vin­di­cated, even after death. For each of them, oth­ers were right and never re­deemed. He guessed that only one in a mil­lion make it. {061-C09}

quote.text: every night I was work­ing grant, grant, grant, and every time the reply came back, no, no, no.

third.head: Small print run, big idea

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Mendel’s forty copies

body: Mendel was an ob­scure monk in Austria, Ajay Shah said, who tried to turn what every plant and an­i­mal breeder knew by in­stinct into laws of in­her­i­tance. He was lucky to choose a sim­ple plant, the pea.

It was one of the most im­por­tant mo­ments in the his­tory of sci­ence, and he pub­lished it qui­etly. Printing was ex­pen­sive: the print run for his paper was 40, all he could af­ford, and he sent copies to a few peo­ple. {061-S10}
Those who read it shrugged, Shah said. Plant breed­ing was noth­ing new to them, and they missed the mag­nif­i­cence of what Mendel had found.
“If bi­ol­ogy has to be more than stamp col­lect­ing,” Shah said, “then it is the child of Mendel and Darwin.” {061-J10}

quote.text: Our species is spe­cial be­cause we are ca­pa­ble of rea­son.

box.title: The book behind the title
box.text: Charlotte Gordon’s *Romantic Outlaws*, a bi­og­ra­phy of mother and daugh­ter, sup­plied “a lot of the dope” for Amit Varma’s first two chap­ters. It shows vividly how hos­tile their world was to women. {061-R01}

sections.label: The mother
sections.head: Taking Locke at his word
sections.caption: Wollstonecraft and the rights of woman
body: Mary Wollstonecraft was born in 1759, Amit Varma said, into times that were not good for women. {#born} Wives could not own prop­erty or ini­ti­ate di­vorce, and it was legal for a hus­band to beat his wife.
She was one of seven chil­dren of an al­co­holic, vi­o­lent fa­ther. Her res­cue came from a neigh­bour, Reverend Henry Clare, who in­tro­duced her to the works of John Locke.
Locke, Varma’s in­tel­lec­tual hero, held that we are all born with the right to self-ownership, from which every other right flows: to free speech, to prop­erty, to life. {061-C02}
## What about women?
Locke also in­spired the American Declaration of Independence. Wollstonecraft, Varma said, read its line that all men are born equal and de­manded to know what was meant by all men. {061-S02}

Her *A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*, in 1792, ar­gued that a false ed­u­ca­tion made women slaves of the male gaze, and that virtue should flow from rea­son, not re­li­gion, tra­di­tion or con­ven­tion. That, Varma said, chal­lenged every con­struct of so­ci­ety. {061-C03}
The book was re­ceived very badly. Thomas Taylor replied with *A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes*: if women can have rights, why not an­i­mals?

~ Varma found one thing tragic. Writing for men who read po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy, she had to argue that freed women would be bet­ter daugh­ters, wives and moth­ers, not that they would live au­ton­o­mous, ful­fill­ing lives.

quote.text: Our species is spe­cial be­cause we are ca­pa­ble of rea­son.

sections.label: The daughter
sections.head: Science fiction from scratch
sections.caption: Frankenstein, written at eighteen
body: Mary Shelley grew up among books, in her fa­ther William Godwin’s salon, and ran away with Percy Shelley, who was al­ready mar­ried.

Around 1816, Amit Varma said, she sat by a fire with Percy Shelley, Lord Byron and John Polidori. Polidori de­scribed the anatomist William Lawrence’s lec­tures ar­gu­ing that there was no soul, only the or­gans of the body. Percy Shelley won­dered whether hu­mans had cre­ated God.
Add John Milton’s *Paradise Lost*, one of her early in­flu­ences, and “you see *Frankenstein* com­ing to birth”, Varma said.

She was eigh­teen. Science fic­tion did not exist, and she had no mod­els of the craft. Yet she told her story in three voices, nested one in­side an­other: a ship’s cap­tain, Frankenstein and his mon­ster.
## Where clichés began
Readers today may find it clumsy and full of clichés. “Do not judge her for those clichés be­cause they started there,” Varma said. “They weren’t clichés there.” {061-C05}

Its ques­tion, whether a being we cre­ate has rights, is live again with ar­ti­fi­cial in­tel­li­gence. “I think the big­gest ques­tions of mod­ern times are ac­tu­ally tack­led by sci­ence fic­tion,” he said. {061-C06}

~ The book was ig­nored, and many as­sumed her hus­band had writ­ten it. Percy Shelley may have writ­ten about 4,000 of its 78,000 words, Varma said, and they stand out as bad writ­ing. {#fourthousand}

quote.text: Here is some­one writ­ing with­out a model for a genre that does not exist, and just com­ing up with a mirac­u­lous book.

sections.label: The doctor
sections.head: Clean hands, dirty politics
sections.caption: Semmelweis and the two maternity wards
body: Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian physi­cian, was born in 1818, the year of *Frankenstein*. In 1846 he joined Vienna General Hospital as an as­sis­tant to the ob­ste­tri­cian, Amit Varma said.
One ma­ter­nity ward had a mor­tal­ity rate of 10 per cent, the other 4 per cent. {#wards} Women begged to be put in the sec­ond.

Overcrowding was not the cause: the safer ward was more crowded. Nor was the weather, since the wards were close to­gether. The clue came when a col­league died after being poked by a scalpel, with the symp­toms of childbed fever. Staff in Ward One also worked on corpses.
## Wash, and live
Semmelweis made them wash their hands in a chlo­ri­nated so­lu­tion. Deaths fell from 18 per cent in one recorded month to two, then one, and to zero within two years. {#eighteen}
But there was no germ the­ory yet. “He solved the prob­lem with­out know­ing why,” Varma said. {061-S05} Doctors, a higher so­cial class, were of­fended at being called un­clean.
One German physi­cian who be­lieved him re­alised a loved one had died be­cause he at­tended her with un­washed hands, and killed him­self. {061-S06}
~ Semmelweis was sacked over de­part­men­tal pol­i­tics. In 1865 he died in a lu­natic asy­lum, of a gan­grenous arm, two weeks after guards beat him and locked him in a dark cell.

quote.text: Am I being blamed for all the deaths that came be­fore?
quote.who: Ajay Shah, voicing the offended doctors

sections.label: The pattern
sections.head: Show me the mechanism
sections.caption: the missing mechanism
body: Why are true ideas re­jected? The re­cur­ring rea­son, Ajay Shah said, is that they work be­fore any­one can ex­plain how. {061-C07}

Semmelweis had no germ the­ory. Alfred Wegener could not say what force moved con­ti­nents. Boltzmann could not show any­one an atom. Darwin’s crit­ics de­manded to see where the code of the finch was writ­ten.

Even a proven fix can wait. Shah re­called the child­hood story of scurvy, solved by car­ry­ing pre­served lime, be­cause sailors lacked only vi­ta­min C. “When you go ex­am­ine the dates care­fully, it’s like decades went by,” he said. {061-S07}
## One fu­neral at a time
Amit Varma cited the Planck prin­ci­ple. Playing the long game, he said, is cold com­fort when, as Keynes put it, in the long run we are all dead. {061-C08}

He had just been in Washington, DC, where his friend Vikram Raghavan pointed out a build­ing in which Keynes had a heart at­tack under a stair­case. “So did he say in the short run we are all dead?” Varma asked. Keynes sur­vived. {061-J05}

~ Shah com­pared Darwin’s delay with Newton, who sat on the cal­cu­lus while Leibniz rushed to pub­lish. “It’s like I’m Newton,” he said. “Once I un­der­stand it, how can hu­mans un­der­stand it?” {061-J04}

quote.text: It re­minds me of the Planck prin­ci­ple, sci­ence changes one fu­neral at a time.

sections.label: The conformists
sections.head: Why the herd bites
sections.caption: the aggressively conventional-minded
body: Amit Varma took his frame from Paul Graham’s essay *The Four Quadrants of Conformism*: peo­ple are con­ven­tional-minded or in­de­pen­dent-minded, and pas­sive or ag­gres­sive. Wallace, Varma said, was ag­gres­sively in­de­pen­dent-minded, Darwin pas­sively so. {061-C10}
Being con­ven­tional-minded he could un­der­stand, as cog­ni­tive lazi­ness or even ra­tio­nal­ity. What flum­moxed him was the ag­gres­sion.

He had met it him­self. When he wrote a col­umn ar­gu­ing that pop­u­la­tion is a good thing, read­ers re­flex­ively at­tacked him in­stead of the ar­gu­ment. School had taught them pop­u­la­tion was the prob­lem, and they had tied the be­lief to them­selves. {061-S14}
## Ridicule at scale

Social media makes it worse, he said. Echoing Adam Mastroianni, he ar­gued that Wegener’s fel­low pro­fes­sion­als may have treated him with dis­dain. “Today the whole world will. And that is such a dis­in­cen­tive.” {061-C11}
Ajay Shah’s an­swer was that peo­ple are tac­itly up­hold­ing a sys­tem of in­sti­tu­tions, cre­den­tials, jour­nals, jobs and fund­ing, and pro­tect­ing their own lives. {061-C12}
Every rung of an aca­demic ca­reer, from school exams to ten­ure, re­wards keep­ing your head down, he said. Of five per­son­al­ity traits, only con­sci­en­tious­ness is se­lected for. {061-C15}
~ His rem­edy was self-interest. We should change our fil­ters, which de­mand a clean shirt, the right jokes and being one of the gang.

quote.text: The very act of imag­i­na­tion, the very act of cre­ativ­ity is prob­a­bly grounded in being a bit of a weirdo
Everyone will say Darwin, wow, Mendel, wow. But there are Darwins and Mendels around us who we prob­a­bly ig­nore and we think of them as weird and we’re not tak­ing them se­ri­ously.

p3.title: Outlaws of science
p3.deck: Four discoveries that came early, and the decades the world took

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the geologist who read a map too well
stories.head: Continents move, minds don’t
body: Alfred Wegener got his idea by star­ing at a map, Ajay Shah said. The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa seemed to fit to­gether like pieces of a jig­saw puz­zle. {061-S08}
“Just imag­ine how many peo­ple would have looked at that same map,” Shah said.

Wegener turned the hunch into testable claims. If the con­ti­nents had once been joined, the fos­sil record should show the same crea­tures on both sides. It did. The rock for­ma­tions should match. They did. He found sim­i­lar cor­re­spon­dences else­where.
He began to dream, Shah said, that about 260 mil­lion years ago all the land was one su­per­con­ti­nent, known as Pangaea, which split apart and drifted. {#pangaea}
His con­tem­po­raries asked for the mech­a­nism: what mighty force could be yank­ing con­ti­nents apart? When he wrote his first book in 1912, it was greeted with de­ri­sion. {#derision}

Amit Varma found that es­pe­cially tragic. Wegener was no out­sider but “a freak­ing ge­ol­o­gist”, think­ing ra­tio­nally, with fos­sils and rock for­ma­tions adding up, re­spected until he went be­yond con­ven­tion.

He kept strug­gling against the es­tab­lish­ment, keen to prove his hy­pothe­ses in Greenland, and died there on an ex­pe­di­tion in 1930. {#greenland} Only in the 1960s did the idea win wide ac­cep­tance, re­cast as plate tec­ton­ics.
~ Shah re­mem­bers it as hot new sci­ence in his father’s day: India split­ting off near Madagascar and smash­ing into Eurasia to push up the Himalayas.
stories.why: The ev­i­dence lay on a map any­one could read. It took one per­son to look, and decades for the field to catch up, be­cause no­body could yet say what moved the con­ti­nents.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Alfred Wegener and the moving continents

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on one theory, cracked twice
stories.head: Twenty-two years and a fever
body: Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle, gath­er­ing spec­i­mens. By 1837, think­ing about the finches and igua­nas of the Galapagos, Ajay Shah said, he had grasped the the­ory of evo­lu­tion.
He also saw at once that it was a per­sonal dis­as­ter. {061-S11} Tell the world that God did not cre­ate us, and they would cut off his head. So he pol­ished his book, year after year.

Darwin, Shah told Amit Varma, “was as great a book writer as you”. {061-J01} Meanwhile Alfred Russel Wallace, deliri­ous with malaria in the jun­gles of Indonesia, cracked the same the­ory from scratch. {#malaria}
~ Wallace, with a bias for ac­tion, came home ready to present. Friends at the Royal Society who knew of Darwin’s se­cret project ar­ranged a joint pre­sen­ta­tion in 1859.

quote.text: And as he un­der­stood it, he also un­der­stood this is a per­sonal dis­as­ter.

stories.postscript: Varma, on Darwin’s 22 years: “I have time, I have time.” {#time}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Darwin, Wallace and evolution

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a physicist who missed his moment
stories.head: Nobody had seen an atom
body: In the 1860s and 1870s, Ajay Shah said, the physi­cist Boltzmann helped make the leap from the ki­netic the­ory of gases, where mol­e­cules are hard dots obey­ing de­ter­min­is­tic rules, to sta­tis­ti­cal me­chan­ics, which uses prob­a­bil­ity through and through.
It ex­plained tem­per­a­ture and en­tropy and gave good pre­dic­tions. But no mi­cro­scope of the late nine­teenth cen­tury could see an atom, and scep­tics asked whether any­one had ever seen one.

Boltzmann had a ter­ri­ble time. He did not get jobs, was thrown out of his home uni­ver­sity in Vienna, and killed him­self in 1906. “And it just is so un­lucky that this was a cou­ple of years be­fore all his stuff worked out,” Shah said. {061-S09}
~ The sto­ries, Shah said, all come from Jacob Bronowski’s book and BBC se­ries *The Ascent of Man*. {061-R13}
stories.why: Being a free thinker, Shah said, is a lonely and chal­leng­ing quest against jobs, ca­reers and an es­tab­lish­ment. Conformity is the easy path. Vindication can ar­rive just after you are gone.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Boltzmann’s unseen atoms

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a disease map that exposed caste
stories.head: Barred from the well, spared
body: In mid-nineteenth-century London, Amit Varma said, John Snow worked out that cholera is caused by water. The find­ing met tremen­dous re­sis­tance, and it took decades, es­pe­cially in India, to be ac­cepted.
Near the end of the cen­tury, an­other in­ves­ti­ga­tor made a cholera map of an Indian vil­lage. It showed that most of those who died were of a higher caste. {061-S12}

The rea­son was a well of con­tam­i­nated water, which the lower castes were not al­lowed to use. “The only per­son from a lower caste who got cholera was a wash­er­man who washed their clothes,” Varma said.
~ These links, he said, were just not ac­cepted. He cred­ited the story to Chinmay Tumbe’s “won­der­ful book”, *Age of Pandemics*. {061-R12}
stories.why: Data can ex­pose a society’s struc­ture as sharply as a disease’s route. Here ex­clu­sion, iron­i­cally, pro­tected the ex­cluded, and even so plain a link took decades to win ac­cep­tance in India.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the cholera map and caste

quiz.q: To which thinker’s works did the neighbour Reverend Henry Clare introduce the young Mary Wollstonecraft?
quiz.a: John Locke, whose phi­los­o­phy grounds every other right in self-ownership.

quiz.q: What did Ignaz Semmelweis make staff do after handling corpses and before examining mothers?
quiz.a: Wash their hands in a chlo­ri­nated so­lu­tion he had pre­pared him­self.

quiz.q: Why was the print run of Mendel’s paper on inheritance in peas only 40?
quiz.a: Printing was ex­pen­sive, and 40 copies were all he could af­ford.

quiz.q: Where was Alfred Russel Wallace when he cracked the theory of evolution from scratch?
quiz.a: In the jun­gles of Indonesia, deliri­ous with a malar­ial fever.

quiz.q: In Paul Graham’s four quadrants, which group poses the greatest danger to new ideas?
quiz.a: The ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded, who react with hos­til­ity to ideas that chal­lenge them.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 61. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. shelf.creator: Charlotte Gordon
shelf.why: A joint bi­og­ra­phy of Mary Wollstonecraft and her daugh­ter Mary Shelley, beau­ti­ful and in­spir­ing lives that show how hos­tile their world was to women: an­i­mals gained legal pro­tec­tion twenty years be­fore the first law lim­it­ing vi­o­lence against women.

shelf.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
shelf.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
shelf.why: The found­ing protofem­i­nist text, writ­ten with no role mod­els: it ap­plies Locke’s nat­u­ral rights to women, ar­gues that a false ed­u­ca­tion makes women slaves of the male gaze and grounds virtue in rea­son.

shelf.title: Frankenstein
shelf.creator: Mary Shelley
shelf.why: Written with no genre or craft mod­els to fol­low, a pi­o­neer­ing work of proto-science fic­tion with an in­no­va­tive nested struc­ture of three nar­ra­tors.

shelf.title: The Book Club, Episode 2: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s short audio in­tro­duc­tion, made for Storytel, to Mary Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: how one of his great he­roes ex­tended Locke’s rights to women and so began mod­ern fem­i­nism.

shelf.title: The Book Club, Episode 3: Frankenstein
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A fif­teen-minute audio take on Frankenstein, to pair with the Wollstonecraft episode.

shelf.title: The Collected Letters of Mary Wollstonecraft
shelf.creator: Mary Wollstonecraft
shelf.why: Amit calls it ‘a beau­ti­ful book’: Wollstonecraft’s inner life in her own words.

shelf.title: Paradise Lost
shelf.creator: John Milton
shelf.why: To see where Frankenstein’s cen­tral ques­tion, a crea­ture con­fronting its cre­ator, comes from.

shelf.title: Blade Runner 2049
shelf.creator: Denis Villeneuve
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite films, which he loves even more than Ridley Scott’s orig­i­nal mas­ter­piece: a mag­nif­i­cent med­i­ta­tion on the shap­ing of the self and the na­ture of mem­ory.

shelf.title: Ex Machina
shelf.creator: Alex Garland
shelf.why: A film that asks whether some­thing we cre­ate that ap­proaches con­scious­ness has rights: if an AGI is con­scious by every def­i­ni­tion we use, why should being made of bits rather than or­ganic mat­ter deny it moral stand­ing?

shelf.title: The Doctors’ Plague
shelf.creator: Sherwin Nuland
shelf.why: The full story of Semmelweis: the dis­cov­ery, the re­jec­tion and the tragic end.

shelf.title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself? (Episode 3, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On whether char­ac­ter is con­tin­gent and whether we can ever know our­selves: a small change in brain chem­istry, as with Phineas Gage, can make you a dif­fer­ent per­son.

shelf.title: Age of Pandemics
shelf.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: Chinmay Tumbe’s his­tory of pan­demics: how cholera’s link to water was found and then re­sisted for decades, es­pe­cially in India, and how past pan­demics ended as strains evolved to­wards less vir­u­lent forms, which is why Amit ex­pected COVID to be­come some­thing we live with.

shelf.title: The Ascent of Man (TV series)
shelf.creator: Jacob Bronowski
shelf.why: A sweep­ing his­tory of sci­en­tific thought that has shaped Ajay since child­hood and is full of sto­ries like these.

shelf.title: The Ascent of Man (book)
shelf.creator: Jacob Bronowski
shelf.why: Bronowski’s his­tory of sci­en­tific thought, the writ­ten com­pan­ion to the TV se­ries that shaped Ajay from child­hood and fed his sto­ries of sci­en­tific out­laws.

shelf.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
shelf.creator: Paul Graham
shelf.why: Paul Graham’s two-axis map of thinkers (con­ven­tional or in­de­pen­dent, pas­sive or ag­gres­sive) that sin­gles out the ag­gres­sively con­ven­tional-minded as the loud­est voices and the real ob­sta­cle to new ideas.

shelf.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s chal­lenge to the school les­son that pop­u­la­tion is India’s big­gest prob­lem: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs, pop­u­la­tion den­sity drives pros­per­ity, and the ills blamed on pop­u­la­tion are fail­ures of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: Who’s Got the Guts to Go to the Moon?
shelf.creator: Adam Mastroianni
shelf.why: Argues that most re­search today is super safe and no­body chases moon­shots.

shelf.title: Emergent Ventures
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: Tyler Cowen’s grant pro­gramme, the orig­i­nal model for fund­ing un­con­ven­tional in­di­vid­u­als; Amit finds it won­der­ful that it backs mad ideas from peo­ple with no cre­den­tials.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
shelf.creator: Mohandas Gandhi
shelf.why: It shows in great de­tail how Gandhi was ‘quite a weirdo’, a re­minder of how un­con­ven­tional great free thinkers look up close.

shelf.title: Newton the Alchemist. Gandhi the Black Swan (Episode 7, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts go under the hood on how Newton and Gandhi emerged, trac­ing their in­tel­lec­tual in­flu­ences rather than judg­ing them by their high­light reels.

shelf.title: Boltzmann’s tombstone in Vienna
shelf.why: Boltzmann’s grave bears his en­tropy equa­tion, S = k ln W, a fit­ting pil­grim­age to an out­law who died just be­fore the world caught up with him.

laughs.text: Ajay on Darwin spend­ing 22 years on his book: ‘Amitbhai, you’ll be pleased to know he was as great a book writer as you.’ Amit: ‘He took a long time, you mean.’ Ajay: ‘He just plod­ded and plod­ded and plod­ded, and he didn’t even have a word pro­ces­sor.’ Later, at ‘22 years’, Amit: ‘I have time, I have time.’

Ajay on Wallace crack­ing evo­lu­tion in a malar­ial delir­ium: ‘Gentle reader, please hope that your cre­ative en­er­gies are fu­eled by malaria... Amitbhai, you may con­sider get­ting a lit­tle malaria to as­sist your project.’
Ajay on Newton sit­ting on the cal­cu­lus while Leibniz rushed to pub­lish: ‘It’s like I’m Newton. Once I un­der­stand it, how can hu­mans un­der­stand it?’

In Washington DC, Amit’s his­tory-obsessed friend Vikram Raghavan points to a build­ing where John Maynard Keynes had a heart at­tack under a stair­case. Amit: ‘So did he say in the short run we are all dead?’ Keynes sur­vived that one.
Amit’s ver­dict on the roughly 4,000 words Percy Shelley con­trib­uted to Frankenstein: they stand out be­cause they’re bad writ­ing, and Shelley’s own nov­els are ‘pretty bad’.
After Ajay says it’s bet­ter to spend an hour with a mad per­son than a sane one, Amit: ‘That’s why I do the show with you.’
Amit, pulling Ajay back to his ques­tion: ‘But that five hun­dred dol­lar bill as five hun­dred dol­lar bills tend to do dis­tracted you.’

Amit pleads for a con­ven­tional rec­om­men­da­tion, be­cause last time Ajay told him to go to ‘Huntsville, Arizona’. Ajay cor­rects him (‘Huntsville, Alabama’) and then rec­om­mends going to a place again: Boltzmann’s tomb­stone in Vienna.
Ajay: ‘If bi­ol­ogy has to be more than stamp col­lect­ing, then it is the child of Mendel and Darwin.’

Thomas Taylor’s mock­ing reply to Wollstonecraft, ‘A Vindication of the Rights of Brutes’: if women get rights, why not an­i­mals? Amit notes that Peter Singer would later make the an­i­mal case se­ri­ously in Animal Liberation.
Horace Walpole’s put-down of Mary Wollstonecraft: ‘a hyena in pet­ti­coats.’

Edmund Burke’s con­ser­va­tive de­fence of tra­di­tion and aris­toc­racy against the French Revolution, an­swered by Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790); Amit notes Thomas Paine’s re­sponse is bet­ter re­mem­bered.
John Locke, now the fa­ther of lib­er­al­ism, was him­self treated as an out­law; Amit be­lieves Cambridge banned him in 1701.

Fritz Lang’s Metropolis, cited as the ori­gin of many cin­e­matic clichés, just as Frankenstein orig­i­nated lit­er­ary ones; Ajay adds the Shakespeare ex­am­ple ‘All that glis­ters is not gold’ (not ‘glitters’).

Amit imag­ines the Wollstonecraft, Shelley and Semmelweis sto­ries as one in­ter­lock­ing web se­ries, a relay race across the dates (Frankenstein and Semmelweis both from 1818) that be­gins and ends with child­birth, hand­wash­ing and death.

entries.clue: Supercontinent Wegener dreamed of, 260 million years ago
Those punished for being ahead of their time
Contaminated source barred to the lower castes
Monk whose pea paper ran to forty copies
Mendel’s lucky choice of simple plant
Ajay prescribed a little for Amit’s creative project
What critics of every outlaw demanded to see
Geologist who saw continents fit like a jigsaw
River Wollstonecraft walked beside in the rain
Mary Shelley’s creation, which tells its own story
He polished his theory for twenty-two years
His principle: science changes one funeral at a time
Alfred Russel, who cracked evolution in a fever
Hungarian doctor who made colleagues wash their hands
Preserved fruit that kept scurvy at bay
